forecaster_note: Surf Guru read: this is the day yesterday's forecast promised, and it delivered. A genuine 12-second SE groundswell at 148–153° is on the coast — 6.8ft at the buoy, 1289 kJ of energy by 10am — with light WNW/NW offshore under it at first light (6–8 kph). That 150° angle is the good one: far enough east of dead south that Dee Why Point actually bends it in instead of the headland eating it. Size is real — Long Reef is 2x overhead (6–10ft), Curl Curl overhead to well overhead (5–8ft), Dee Why a more workable 5–7ft, North Steyne the manageable 4–6ft. The catch is the clock: wind is dead-light WNW/NW until about 9am, swings N at 10am (8 kph gusting 16), NE by noon (13 kph gusting 17) and ENE 19 gusting 24 by 4pm. So it's a dawn-to-10am session, full stop. Tide sits low at 4:27am and fills to a 1.35m high at 10:35am, which softens the banks right as the swell peaks — good news at Curl Curl, less relevant at the Point. Water 19.2°C (SharkSmart station median, 53 stations), air only 13°C at 9am under clear sky. Monday collapses: 3.8ft at 10s and 146 kJ, 2–4ft and fun-sized at best. 🦈 SharkSmart NSW read clean — no detections Palm Beach → Manly in the last 24h across all five feeds. ✈️ Reminder: you're in Oahu until 13 Aug, so this one runs without you — use /hawaii-surf over there. ⚠️ Note: this note is composed from live Surfline point data (wave / wind / tide / weather JSON), not quoted from a Surfline forecaster; the free forecast window ends Fri 7 Aug, so the weekend tab is a trend projection, not a live read.

wind.summary: Dead-light WNW/NW offshore at dawn — 7 kph at 6am, 6 gusting 10 at 9am. Then it turns fast: N at 10am (8 gusting 16), NE by noon (13 gusting 17), ENE 19 gusting 24 by 4pm. Dawn to 10am is the whole window today.

shark.summary: No shark detections logged anywhere between Palm Beach and Manly in the last 24 hours. SMART drumline (349 features), DPI/SLS drone (82), Surf Life Saving NSW (144), trauma (7) and events (1) feeds all read clean this refresh.

days.label: Today
days.note: The best swell of the fortnight with the shortest window to use it. 6.8ft at 12 seconds from 150° SE, 1289 kJ by 10am, 98% consistency — and light WNW/NW offshore that folds to N at 10am and NE onshore by noon. Dawn to 10am or it's gone. The 10:35am high fills in right as the swell peaks, which helps the open beaches more than the Point. Size is genuinely big at the Reef — pick your spot to match your appetite, not your ego.

swells.label: The engine — 12s at 150°, the angle that actually wraps into the Point
Afternoon NE windchop — arrives with the sea breeze, adds nothing

dee-why.window: Best quality-to-consequence call of the four and the only one rating GOOD. 6–9am under the WNW/NW offshore is the session — 5–7ft with a proper 12-second wall behind it. Energy actually climbs from 582 kJ at 8am to 1289 by 10am, so the last hour before the wind turns is the heaviest and the best. After 10am the N/NE gets into it and it's over.
alerts: Hard stop at 10am — wind swings N (8 gusting 16) then NE by noon. This is not a dawn-to-lunch day.

tip.label: Frontside tip
tip.text: Frontside at the Point and the swell direction is finally on your side — 150° with 12 seconds behind it is exactly what the headland is shaped to bend. Unlike last weekend's 9-second slop, this one gives you a real wall, so commit to the bottom turn and drive off it rather than rushing to the pocket. 1289 kJ at 5–7ft means the sets have serious push: sit deeper than feels comfortable and take the first one of the set, because the second and third stand up further inside.

swells.label: The engine — the Reef takes a 150° SE full in the chest

long-reef.window: Biggest of the four by a distance and the only serious wave on the coast today. 6–9am is the whole window — offshore is straightest early and the energy is still climbing. Rates fair-to-good rather than good purely because 6–10ft on a 12-second SE is more consequence than most sessions are worth.
alerts: 6–10ft double-overhead with 1289 kJ behind it on a genuine long-period groundswell. Step-up board, known channel, and don't paddle out alone.
Energy climbs through the morning while the wind deteriorates — it gets heavier as it gets worse. First light or not at all.

tip.label: Frontside tip
tip.text: The Reef corner is your frontside. On a 12-second SE the sets refract wide and land further up the point than a short-period swell — sit north of the usual take-off and let the first wave of each set go through so you can read where the bowl is actually breaking. Step up on volume: at this size you cannot stall your way into the drop, you have to be moving before it lifts.

swells.label: The engine — straight into the open Curl Curl banks with nothing in the way

curl-curl.window: A lot of water on an open beachbreak — 5–8ft with no headland to organise it. The 10:35am high is the saving grace here more than anywhere else, because it stops a 12-second swell squaring up on the sandbanks. North Curl Curl corner is the read; go 8–10am on the tide push and accept you'll spend time paddling.
alerts: Open beachbreak at 5–8ft on a 12-second period — expect long closeout sets and a serious rip. Find the channel before you get wet.

tip.label: Backside tip
tip.text: North Curl Curl's lefts are your backhand and at this size the corner is the only sane part of the beach. Twelve seconds gives you a wall that actually runs, which is the opposite problem to last weekend — set the rail early off the drop and hold your line rather than pumping. If the corner is closing out on the low tide push, wait for the 10:35am high instead of drifting south into open beach.

swells.label: The engine — North Steyne sits deepest in the shadow, which today is the point

manly.window: The sane option. Half of Long Reef's size but the same 12-second period and the same 1289 kJ behind it, so the waves still have real push — just at a size you can surf rather than survive. Clean under the WNW/NW until 10am. This is the pick if you want a full session instead of three good waves and a beating.

tip.label: Backside tip
tip.text: Backhand on the North Steyne lefts. Chest-to-overhead with 1289 kJ behind it hits harder than the size suggests — the take-off will pitch more than you expect for a 4–6ft wave. Ride volume rather than a step-up here; you want paddle speed to get into them early, then let the 12-second wall do the work down the line.

days.label: Tomorrow
days.note: The bill for today. Swell collapses to 3.8ft at 10 seconds from 146° with only 146 kJ behind it — a fifth of today's energy — and keeps easing through the day (199 kJ at 6am down to 81 by 3pm). Consistency is a perfect 100%, so it's reliable, just small. Wind is friendly for once: NNW 6–10 kph in the morning, WNW by midday, no real sea breeze. A tiny 20-second S background pulse (0.5ft) is the only hint of anything new. Fun-sized groveller day, not a session to plan around.

dee-why.window: Small but clean all morning — NNW offshore at 6 kph dawn, easing WNW by midday, and no sea breeze to chase you out. The Point won't have much to bend at 10 seconds and 146°, so the open banks are the better read. Any time before 1pm works; the tide matters more than the clock today.

long-reef.window: Still the size leader and today that's a virtue rather than a warning — 3–6ft with the leftover 20-second S pulse underneath. The most likely spot to still have a proper wave on it. Morning offshore is light and clean.

curl-curl.window: Wide range because the banks are doing all the work at this size. North Curl Curl corner on the tide push, otherwise it's a paddle. Clean under the NNW all morning.

manly.window: Deepest in the shadow of a 146° swell that's already run out of energy. Thigh-to-stomach and soft. Only worth it if you're already down here.

days.label: Weekend
days.note: PROJECTION, NOT A LIVE READ — Surfline's free forecast window ends Fri 7 Aug, so the coming weekend sits beyond the data. What the model does show is a southerly groundswell building hard through the back half of the week: Thu 6 Aug brings 5.8ft at 9s from 177° (762 kJ) and Fri 7 Aug climbs to 7.6ft at 10s from 174° (1037 kJ), both with W/WSW offshore in the mornings. That's a dead-south angle — 174–177° is the direction that wraps badly at Dee Why and over-favours Long Reef and Curl Curl. If the pattern holds, expect the weekend to open with easing south swell and offshore mornings; if a new low forms it could rebuild. Re-check this tab from Thursday when the real numbers come into range.

dee-why.window: Projected easing south swell behind Friday's 7.6ft peak, with W offshore mornings. A 174–177° angle is the one that gets eaten by the headland here, so expect Dee Why to under-perform its neighbours — the open banks over the Point.
